The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings

I t could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.

Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.

Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “ No, I don’t think so. ” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.

Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “ special relationship ” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.

Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up . These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

stories.title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
stories.summary: Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.

Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.

“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.

Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling

Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

“The contracts which Plaintiff mischaracterizes as gambling are event contracts offered on the Platform subject to the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act], in conformance with the rules and regulations of the CFTC [Commodity Futures Trading Commission], the federal agency which has statutory authority to oversee the CEA,” Kalshi said.

We contacted Bright’s attorney, Michael Daudt, about Kalshi’s court filings and will update this article if we get a response.

“Plaintiff alleges that his activity on the platform was gambling and that he ‘lost,’” Kalshi wrote. “He does not allege that anyone misled him about how the platform worked, what it charged, or the risk that any position might lose. Yet, he now sues KalshiEX and its parent, Kalshi Inc., to recover nearly double his own alleged net realized loss under Washington’s gambling loss-recovery statute, and a theory of unjust enrichment.”

Between June 17 and August 14, 2026, Bright transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi in 253 separate debits from his checking account, his lawsuit said. Kalshi allegedly collected $5,589.05 in funding fees on those transfers.

Bright made numerous wagers on sporting events including professional baseball games and tennis matches. He apparently put any winnings into new bets, and alleges that “Kalshi’s platform cycled Plaintiff’s deposits through $14,396,457.30 in transactions and assessed and retained $84,062.71 in trading fees on them, equal to 26.7 percent of everything Plaintiff deposited.”

After all his bets, Bright suffered a net loss of $308,781.62, and his account was left with a balance of $983.27. Kalshi said that Bright’s “alleged losses went to counterparties rather than” to Kalshi itself and that Bright’s “positions were matched with counterparties and resolved according to the outcomes of the underlying events.”

“The Complaint does not allege that KalshiEX or Kalshi Inc. was the counterparty to any of Plaintiff’s positions,” Kalshi said.

Kalshi calls itself “a neutral exchange platform” with no financial stake in the outcome of any event. It makes revenue by collecting fees on transactions. But while Kalshi describes itself as a neutral operator and collector of transaction fees, its business model also includes a trading affiliate that places wagers on the platform.

Kalshi’s trading affiliate

Kalshi’s rulebook says its trading affiliate “participates on the Platform and provides liquidity to the Platform by placing orders on either (or both) sides of a market at competitive price levels.” Kalshi says its affiliate only has access to the same public information that other traders on the platform have.

Bright’s lawsuit alleges that Kalshi’s affiliate “took the opposite side of a substantial portion of Plaintiff’s positions,” meaning that “Kalshi and the enterprise under common ownership with it were not a neutral venue but the dealer or player winning within the meaning of [state law], in addition to being the proprietor for whose benefit the wagering was conducted.”

Bright doesn’t know for sure whether Kalshi’s affiliate was on the other side of any of his bets. “The identity of the participant on the opposite side of each of Plaintiff’s positions, and the profit each such participant realized, is information exclusively within Kalshi’s possession,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws. Although that case involved Nevada, the Ninth Circuit’s jurisdiction includes the state of Washington. Bright’s lawsuit quoted the ruling’s finding that “placing sports bets, even when called by another name, is still gambling.”

Although Bright’s lawsuit said his net loss was $308,781.62, he asked for $580,544.98 based on an “event-by-event” calculation derived from a 1950 ruling issued by the Washington Supreme Court. “Computed on the event-by-event basis required by Heitfeld , under which winnings in separate and distinct events may not be offset against losses, the sums Plaintiff lost total $580,544.98,” the lawsuit said.

Bright’s lawsuit said that if the court declines to order $580,544.98 in restitution, it should instead award “all funds Plaintiff transferred to Kalshi and the $89,651.76 in funding and trading fees Kalshi collected.” That would amount to over $405,000.

Kalshi seeks delay until Supreme Court weighs in

In addition to its motion to dismiss the case, Kalshi filed a motion to stay the proceedings at least until the US Supreme Court decides whether to take up a separate case on whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets. “The orderly course of justice favors a stay because Supreme Court review will settle or simplify every claim and ensure uniform treatment of like suits,” Kalshi told the US district court.

Kalshi has suffered some notable losses in US appeals courts, which found that states can regulate the platform’s event contracts under gambling laws. But federal courts have not unanimously sided with states, and New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to settle the question of whether states can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws.

Kalshi’s motion for a stay in the Bright case noted that Washington government officials are “pursuing overlapping claims” against Kalshi. “The State of Washington is pursuing the same theory, and seeks the same recovery for Mr. Bright, in a case pending before the Superior Court of Washington for King County,” Kalshi wrote.

Kalshi tried to get the state’s case moved to a federal court, but it was sent back to King County Superior Court in May. Washington won a preliminary injunction against Kalshi in August, when a King County judge ordered Kalshi to implement geofencing and stop allowing many types of wagers in the state.

The county court’s order required Kalshi to stop offering or accepting event contracts “related to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions” in the state. The injunction did not affect wagers in the commodities, climate, economics, and finance categories.

Bright transferred his funds to Kalshi before the geofencing order took effect. His lawsuit claims that on September 15, he tried to access the app but received a notice that “using this app in your current location is prohibited.”

This article was updated to correct the date the lawsuit was filed .

"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang

Published 9 November 2026

US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

The company is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as its share price fell by more than 4%.

Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Published 2 hours ago

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 6 hours ago

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips. She is not related to the Nvidia chief.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

The American firm, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security.

Huang and Nvidia were also sued on Monday in a proposed class action lawsuit in California accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing the chief executive's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the firm lied to the media about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

'He said he had no idea she was a spy'

At the White House, Trump was asked multiple times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

Trump said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president said.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Nvidia designs advanced computer chips that power AI models and is at the centre of the US and China's technology race - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked national security fears.

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Huang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

It is unclear whether Huang will appear. Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 4 hours ago

AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values Published 3 days ago

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday told the BBC that it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

Closing summary

Shares of Nvidia tumbled 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation on Sunday came after its boss admitted that he had an affair with Alice Huang , an executive at Singapore-based datacenter company Megaspeed, who according to the New York Times , US intelligence determined was gathering information for China. The episode has thrown Jensen Huang’s future at the company – and that of Nvidia itself – up in the air, and raises serious questions about US national security – given Jensen Huang’s close relationship with Donald Trump – and what Alice Huang could have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair.

The New York Times reported in ​October that Trump was briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing, but the US president did not act on it. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I have not ​spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.” Trump later added: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” He said he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

The New York Times also reported on Monday that a US commerce department investigation into Megaspeed – the data company led by Alice Huang – was halted after Nvidia’s general counsel intervened. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, reportedly contacted the investigators at commerce department to inform them that their boss, Jeff Kessler – a top official – had given Teter permission to request details about their probe into Megaspeed. The case focused on whether the company was smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China. According to current and former government officials, and others familiar with the incident, that the NYT spoke to, some viewed Kessler’s interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the investigation. The case was eventually transferred to the US justice department late last year, but questions remain about Kessler’s discussions with Nvidia, and what information he subsequently relayed to Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary or the wider Trump administration. According to the Times’ sources, the justice department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed.

US Republican lawmakers expressed alarm over the episode, asking Jensen Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, currently the House minority leader who is poised to become new Speaker next year, said that he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill. “Clearly Congress needs more information,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation.”

Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls, meanwhile, expressed their support for the embattled Nvidia CEO. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”. “Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. “Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post. Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair. Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

There’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., saying that Huang is “not replaceable.” “On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives wrote.

The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare said that Nvidia was being treated as a one-off story by investors for the moment. “In other words, the stock is being penalised for Jensen Huang’s personal transgression, which has invited a great deal of uncertainty into the mix, but the market isn’t caught up in the notion that this situation is going to have a systemic domino effect,” he said.

The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Over in the US Congress, Hakeem Jeffries , currently the House minority leader who is poised to become its new Speaker next year, has said ⁠that Congress ⁠needs answers after reports emerged ⁠ Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted ⁠by a foreign ​intelligence ‌effort.

Jeffries ‌also said he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill.

“ Clearly Congress needs more information ,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation. ”

The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

Aisha Down and Dan Milmo

Reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort are a big deal, given Jensen Huang ’s close relationship with the US president.

Aside from Jensen Huang’s dented personal reputation after admitting to having an affair with Alice Huang – an alleged Chinese spy - what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?

The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.

Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang, a Megaspeed executive, had formed a “close relationship” with Ms Huang and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.

At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed . That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.

Further, Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – with the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.

Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships : the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.

The US president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports . The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.

Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.

But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.

What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.

Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, on stage in London.

He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.

For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

As we’ve been reporting, shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang , was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Further to my last post regarding succession at Nvidia, there’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., told the Associated Press that Huang is “not replaceable”.

“On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave [in the US midterm elections] this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives said.

Still, Ives said there is a risk, as Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board’s investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.

Opinion: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang , the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal . The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined .

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

But legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct ? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump . “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire , a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

Nvidia ’s embattled CEO Jensen Huang has disappeared from the line-up of two tech events he was due to speak at this week, according to Business Insider (paywall) .

Insider reports: “Ahead of its expected IPO next week, Anthropic is hosting a private CEO forum this week in Montecito. Huang was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive on Monday evening, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. He is no longer expected to attend, according to a second person familiar with the matter.”

Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?

There is little public information available about Alice Huang , the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations , a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.

She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.

US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang , the chief executive of Nvidia, the chip company critical to US ambitions to stay ahead of China in the AI race.

People briefed on the US intelligence told the New York Times they believed Alice Huang was recruited as part of efforts to learn more about American AI chips, and to try to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be made available to China.

China has denied the allegations, calling them “nothing but smears”.

It is unclear exactly when the two Huangs, who are not related, first met.

Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected within the upper echelons of the global AI chip industry, the New York Times wrote, citing people who had met her.

Megaspeed , the datacentre company for which she was previously listed as chief executive, still describes itself as “a premier business partner of Nvidia” on LinkedIn.

It was in this capacity that the businesswoman was pictured in Jensen Huang’s company several times in 2024 and 2025.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted by another attending company on LinkedIn, shows the two sitting next to each other on a couch in Taipei.

The year after, they were filmed together again in Taipei at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Press outside livestreamed footage of the two, seemingly comfortable in each other’s company, with Jensen Huang at one point putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek.

The two later left the restaurant in the same car, the footage showed.

A New York-based short-selling firm first raised concerns publicly about their “uncomfortably close relationship” six months ago.

Earlier this year, US officials wrote a memo saying the two Huangs had been romantically involved, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing sources who had seen it.

On Sunday the Nvidia chief executive sent a company-wide email apologising for an affair.

He did not name Alice Huang but said he would cooperate with an investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports”.

Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and she has not given a public statement about the allegations.

It is unclear what her current relationship is with Megaspeed, though Culper Research, the short-selling firm, quoted an employee in May as saying that contrary to public reporting, Alice Huang was “actually still our boss”.

The details of her career before that are difficult to ascertain.

Several media outlets have cited a profile matching her name and picture on a Chinese fund database, which listed previous jobs at banks including HSBC and CITIC, as well as roles at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

However, reporters have been unable to confirm any of the details listed.

Megaspeed is among a number of south-east Asian firms that buy chips to build facilities and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

According to Singapore’s the Straits Times, it was previously known as 7Road International – a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors.

At the time of the rebrand, it was owned by Huang Le Limited and led by Alice Huang, the newspaper said, before the ownership was transferred to another company in 2023.

Since late 2024, the US government has reportedly been investigating Megaspeed for helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions.

The New York Times said Singapore questioned Alice Huang during its own investigation into the company, but released her.

Nvidia has previously said it has looked into Megaspeed but found no cause for concern.

The Guardian has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy

Donald Trump , Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

“ I have not ​spoken to him about it ,” the US president told reporters on Sunday.

double quotation mark I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.

“ I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it ,” Trump later added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the United States, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “ I agree ” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire ’s defense of Huang.

“ Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership ,” Maguire posted. He stated the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“ Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op ,” Maguire added in a separate post.

Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.

“ He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes ,” Ackman posted. “ He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward. ”

Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security” .

Investigators at the US commerce department had been looking into a Singaporean company suspected of smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China last year, the New York Times reports.

The probe came to an abrupt end when it was transferred instead to the justice department, following an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information.

The investigation was centred on data centre company Megaspeed, led by an executive now believed to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang.

The NYT reports:

double quotation mark It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company’s representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler’s interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident.

Nvidia'’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.

“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Nvidia’s shares pared losses from an 8% slide to now down 6%, extending last week’s selloff ‌and pushing the stock to fresh multi-month lows.

At current levels, ‌the chipmaker would lose more than $280 billion in value from its last closing price, Reuters reports.

Summary

Shares of Nvidia tumbled 5% at the opening bell Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation on Sunday followed Huang’s acknowledgment that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to the New York Times, US intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”

Republican lawmakers have expressed alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.

Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions. “I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.

There’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., saying that Huang is “not replaceable.” “On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives wrote.

The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Meanwhile, technology analyst Dan Ives, at the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the crisis would at the very least spark congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons”.

“This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” Ives said.

“This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC,” he added.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Published 9 November 2026

One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

On Sunday, Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair .

The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.

Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 59 minutes ago

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 4 hours ago

Who is Alice Huang and what do we know about the affair?

Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - pictured at an event

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

China has rejected the spying allegations.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."

The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.

Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times.

Nvidia shares slide as US tech giant investigates CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Published 16 September

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? Published 14 September

Why does it matter?

Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang has soared to international importance with his company

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

What is Nvidia and how important is it?

There is no clear successor for Huang at Nvidia

Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates .

Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips.

Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever.

For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.

There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.

His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.

Who is Jensen Huang's wife?

Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September

Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

Nvidia is probing whether Chinese intelligence targeted its CEO through an affair.

Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China.

Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document.

The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company.

It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off.

Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday.

Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer.

The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping.

Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security.

Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added.

After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday.

He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025.

The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration.

The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation.

“The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO.

Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running.

He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today.

Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”

But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.”

stories.title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today , along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places. But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment. We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant. Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay SIREN and CAIR-CA v. San Jose

stories.body:
Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision

For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.

But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair.

Initially , Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader.

Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton.

Spencer , for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan.

Could Jensen Huang be pushed out?

In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation.

“This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”

Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board.

“The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.”

after newsletter promotion

Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said.

“Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.”

Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate.

Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly.

Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value.

“When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. “It’s not just a question of romance or morality any more. It’s a question of judgment, national security exposure, shareholder trust, and whether the person at the top can be relied on to protect the enterprise.”

In a statement, Nvidia’s board said they do not believe either national security or company secrets were compromised but they will “examine all available information.”

“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” the board said in a statement .

stories.title: Why are hundreds of prisoners being released early?
stories.summary: More people going to prison, and for longer, is why governments including the current one have had to release prisoners early.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 August 2026

Around 650 more prisoners in England and Wales are due to be released on Tuesday under the third tranche of the government's early release scheme.

Under the scheme, eligible prisoners are released after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of the term.

People sentenced for manslaughter, rape, and serious child sex and grooming offences are excluded.

This is not the first time a government - Conservative or Labour - has released prisoners early to make space in England and Wales' overcrowded prisons.

BBC Verify has looked at the reasons why ministers say the current scheme is necessary.

More prisoners than prison space

The prison population in England and Wales on 9 November was 86,982, which was 97.6% of useable capacity , external .

In the long-term the MoJ has projected that the capacity of all prisons will rise to around 99,000 by 2032 as a result of more prisons being built by this government.

But it also projected that the prisoner population would rise to about 104,000 by 2032 if the Sentencing Act 2026 - which provides for earlier release - did not come into force.

That is why Justice Secretary Alex Norris says there is a "prison capacity crisis" which means the government has to implement the latest early release scheme.

In total 4,500 prisoners are due to be released early by June 2027 , external . The first tranche saw about 700 offenders released from jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

The MoJ has projected that the Sentencing Act will mean the prisoner population remains below the capacity of the prison system, rising only to around 96,000 by 2032.

More people are being sent to prison for longer

The England and Wales prison population has risen significantly in recent decades with a significant uptick starting in the 1990s before reaching a record high in 2024.

The Institute for Government (IFG) think tank says this is partly the result of longer sentences.

In 2023, the average prison sentence at Crown Courts in England and Wales - which deal with more serious offences - was more than 25% longer than those handed down in 2012.

For some crimes, the increase was greater. Sentences for robbery in 2023 were 13 months longer on average than in 2012 - an increase of 36%.

Longer sentences mean more people being held in prison at any one time.

Former Conservative Justice Secretary David Gauke, who led an independent sentencing review for Sir Keir Starmer's government, argues this is the result of a "bidding war" by political parties since the 1990s over who can imprison people for longer.

Gauke also points out that the prison population has been rising at a time when overall crime in England and Wales has been falling, according to the official Crime Survey.

So despite the fall in crime more people are being sent to prison - and for longer.

Another reason for upward pressure on the prison population is that more people than before are being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Cassia Rowland from the IFG said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

Slow pace of prison building

Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises.

Between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power, around 13,000 new prison places were created.

But around 12,500 places - notably those built during the Victorian era - were closed after falling into disrepair.

That means an estimated net total of only around 500 new prison places were added over 14 years.

In a 2024 report, the National Audit Office (NAO) cited the MOJ's "unrealistic timelines", and government bodies not working together to prioritise delivery, as reasons for the slow pace of prison building.

Work is under way on a new prison - HMP Welland - being built in Leicestershire

The MOJ say around 6,500 net prison places were created between 2022 and 2025, once closures are taken into consideration. These include places created in three new prisons.

However, further expansion to existing prisons has been delayed by a major supplier going into administration, according to the Prison Reform Trust.

Pia Sinha of the Prison Reform Trust told BBC Verify: "Successive governments have found it difficult to increase prison capacity because new prisons take years to plan and build, often facing planning hurdles and local opposition."

The Labour government has pledged to build 14,000 new prison places by 2031.

Analysts argue that without a major change in thinking about the appropriateness of prison as punishment, or a significant long-term increase in prison building, the system in England and Wales will remain close to capacity.

And that means governments will continue to be under pressure to implement early release schemes to avert a capacity crisis.
